title: What Is Deep Learning?
content:
Deep learning is a subfield of machine learning that uses artificial
neural networks with multiple layers to learn complex patterns from data.
Each layer transforms its input into a more useful representation for
the next layer. Unlike traditional machine learning, deep learning can
automatically learn features from raw data, reducing the need for manual
feature engineering. It is widely used in computer vision, natural
language processing, speech recognition, and generative AI.

title: Artificial Neural Networks
content:
An artificial neural network consists of interconnected neurons organized
into input, hidden, and output layers. Each neuron calculates a weighted
sum of its inputs, adds a bias, and applies an activation function.
During training, the network adjusts its weights and biases to minimize
a loss function. Neural networks can model nonlinear relationships and
serve as the foundation for architectures such as convolutional neural
networks, recurrent neural networks, and transformers.

title: Forward Propagation
content:
Forward propagation is the process of passing input data through a neural
network to produce a prediction. At each layer, the network multiplies
the input by a weight matrix, adds a bias vector, and applies an
activation function. The final layer produces the model output, which
can represent a class probability or a numerical prediction. The loss
function then measures the difference between this prediction and the
actual target. Forward propagation is performed during both training
and inference.

title: Backpropagation and Gradient Descent
content:
Backpropagation calculates how much each model parameter contributes
to the prediction error by applying the chain rule of calculus.
It computes gradients of the loss with respect to the weights and biases.
Gradient descent then uses these gradients to update the parameters
in a direction that reduces the loss. The learning rate controls the
size of each update. Backpropagation calculates gradients, while the
optimizer uses those gradients to update model parameters. Both are
essential parts of training neural networks.

title: Activation Functions
content:
Activation functions introduce nonlinear behavior into neural networks,
allowing them to learn complex relationships. ReLU returns the input
when it is positive and zero otherwise. Sigmoid maps values into the
interval between zero and one and is often used for binary classification
outputs. Softmax converts a vector of logits into a probability
distribution across multiple classes. The choice of activation function
depends on the network architecture and prediction task.

title: Loss Functions in Deep Learning
content:
A loss function measures how different a model's predictions are from
the expected targets. Mean squared error is commonly used for regression,
while binary cross-entropy is suitable for binary classification and
categorical cross-entropy is commonly used for multiclass classification.
The training process attempts to minimize the selected loss. Choosing
an appropriate loss function depends on the task, target representation,
and model output layer.

title: Overfitting and Regularization
content:
Overfitting occurs when a model learns patterns specific to its training
data, including noise, and performs poorly on unseen examples. A common
sign is a low training loss combined with a substantially higher
validation loss. Regularization techniques help reduce overfitting.
These include L1 and L2 penalties, dropout, data augmentation, early
stopping, and reducing model complexity. Evaluating performance on
separate validation and test sets helps estimate generalization.

title: Convolutional Neural Networks
content:
Convolutional neural networks are designed to process grid-like data,
especially images. Convolutional layers apply learnable filters to
detect local patterns such as edges, textures, and shapes. Pooling or
strided convolutions can reduce spatial dimensions, while deeper layers
learn increasingly complex representations. CNNs are widely used for
image classification, object detection, segmentation, and medical image
analysis. Their shared weights make them more parameter-efficient than
fully connected networks for many image-processing tasks.

title: Transfer Learning and Fine-Tuning
content:
Transfer learning reuses knowledge learned by a model on one task for
another related task. A common approach is to start with a pretrained
network, freeze its backbone, and train a new classification head.
Fine-tuning goes further by unfreezing some or all pretrained layers
and updating their parameters on the target dataset. Transfer learning
is especially useful when labeled data or computational resources are
limited. A smaller learning rate is often used during fine-tuning to
avoid destroying useful pretrained representations.

title: Transformers and Self-Attention
content:
Transformers process sequences using attention mechanisms rather than
relying primarily on recurrent connections. Self-attention allows each
token to assign different importance to other tokens in the sequence.
Query, key, and value projections are used to calculate attention
weights and combine information from different positions. Multi-head
attention learns several attention patterns in parallel, while
positional information helps the model represent token order.
Transformers are widely used in large language models, machine
translation, document understanding, and multimodal AI.

title: Batch Normalization and Dropout
content:
Batch normalization normalizes intermediate activations using statistics
from training batches and learnable parameters. It can improve training
stability and sometimes allow higher learning rates. Dropout randomly
disables a fraction of activations during training to reduce reliance
on particular neurons. During inference, dropout is disabled, while
batch normalization uses its accumulated running statistics. These
techniques address different issues and may be used together depending
on the architecture.

title: Evaluating Classification Models
content:
Classification models can be evaluated using accuracy, precision,
recall, F1-score, and a confusion matrix. Accuracy measures the fraction
of predictions that are correct. Precision measures how many predicted
positives are actually positive, while recall measures how many actual
positives are detected. The F1-score is the harmonic mean of precision
and recall. For imbalanced datasets, accuracy alone can be misleading,
so precision, recall, F1-score, and per-class metrics may provide a
more useful assessment.
